I have been farming these lands in Quzhou for over forty years. At sixty-five, I have seen the good years and the bad, and I know what this soil can do. I finished high school — not many of my generation in the village did — so I can read the county's agricultural bulletins and I pay attention to what the extension agents say. But in the end, I trust my own eyes and the experience of working this ground season after season.

The North China Plain gives us a short summer and a cold winter, but the heat and light between June and September are enough for a full maize crop if we move fast. That is why I stick to the wheat–maize double-cropping system on my best land. I have eight *mu* of flat, well-drained fields that I will plant to winter wheat this October and follow immediately with summer maize next June. The other three *mu* I will put into cotton. Cotton is more work — it needs spraying almost every week once the bolls open — but the price has been steady, and it spreads my risk if grain prices fall.

For the wheat, I will use an improved variety that the seed station recommends. It is not the newest hybrid, but it is hardy and the quality is good enough for the grain buyer. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and level the field. I will put down compound fertilizer as a basal dressing — about fifty *jin* per *mu* — and then top-dress with urea at the green-up and jointing stages. In total that gives me roughly thirty kilograms of nitrogen per *mu*, which is what this soil needs after maize has taken its share. I will irrigate four times: at green-up in March, at jointing, at heading, and once more at grain-filling if the spring is dry. I expect about five hundred kilograms per *mu* if the weather cooperates.

The maize is different. After we harvest the wheat in early June, we have maybe ten days before the maize must be in the ground. There is no time for ploughing. I will plant hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble — no-tillage — and side-dress with urea when the plants reach knee-height. I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing to help emergence, and again at the tasseling stage. The hybrid should give me around six hundred kilograms per *mu*.

The cotton goes on the smaller plot with rotary tillage in spring. I use an improved cotton variety and apply a modest amount of compound fertilizer at planting. I will irrigate twice during the peak flowering period and spray for bollworm and aphids about fifteen times through the season. I expect roughly two hundred eighty kilograms of seed cotton per *mu*.

This is the plan I will follow. It is what I know works here.
